Falsely
FAWLS-lee
adv. (untruly, with intent to deceive; rendering Hebrew sheqer used adverbially, Greek pseudomenoi)
From Latin falsus, past participle of fallere, to deceive. The adverb is the legal form of the word: it describes not a mistaken statement but a statement made against known truth, usually under oath or against a neighbour.

Biblical Definition

Falsely is a courtroom and covenant word. Its home is the ninth commandment and the law of oaths, where Leviticus states the two prohibitions together: “Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another” (Leviticus 19:11), and then raises the stakes by attaching the Name: “ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:12). A false oath is not merely a lie told to a man; it is a profanation, because it calls God as witness to a thing God knows to be untrue. Jeremiah finds a whole religious economy built on the practice and traces the corruption from the top down and the bottom up at once: “The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so: and what will ye do in the end thereof?” (Jeremiah 5:31). The clergy lie, the priests profit by it, and the people prefer it — a false ministry always has a constituency. The Lord Jesus then turns the word around and makes it a beatitude: the disciples are blessed when men “shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Matthew 5:11), with the qualifier falsely doing essential work, since there is no blessing on reproach a man has earned. Paul applies the adverb to a whole discipline: “oppositions of science falsely so called” (1 Timothy 6:20) — knowledge wearing the name of knowledge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Untruly, against known truth. Leviticus binds it to the Name in the law of oaths; Jeremiah shows a whole priesthood profiting by it while the people prefer it; Christ blesses only reproach that is false; Paul names knowledge falsely so called.

expand to see more

FALSELY, adv. In a manner contrary to truth and fact; not truly; erroneously.

2. Treacherously; perfidiously. He falsely betrayed his trust.

3. Insincerely; not honestly; as, he falsely professed friendship.

4. Contrary to the true and proper sense of the term; as, science falsely so called. 1 Tim. 6.

FALSE, a. [L. falsus, from fallo, to deceive.] Not true; not conformable to fact; expressing what is contrary to that which exists, is done, said or thought.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 19:11 — "Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another."

Leviticus 19:12 — "And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD."

Jeremiah 5:31 — "The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so: and what will ye do in the end thereof?"

Matthew 5:11 — "Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake."

Modern Corruption

The qualifier is dropped from Matthew 5:11, so that opposition of any kind is claimed as persecution for Christ's sake — and 1 Timothy 6:20 is meanwhile used to dismiss real knowledge rather than the counterfeit Paul actually named.

expand to see more

Matthew 5:11 contains a word that is almost always omitted when the verse is claimed: falsely, and with it the phrase for my sake. The Lord blesses those slandered by lies on His account. He does not bless the man whose obnoxiousness has earned him the criticism he receives, and Peter draws the line explicitly — let none suffer as a busybody in other men's matters, but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed (1 Peter 4:15-16). The habit of treating every rebuke as evidence of faithfulness is an effective way to become unteachable, and it borrows the language of martyrdom to do it. The test is simple and is written in the text: is the accusation false, and is it on account of Christ?

Paul's phrase in 1 Timothy 6:20 is likewise abused. Science falsely so called is the Greek pseudonymos gnosis — knowledge wearing a name that does not belong to it, aimed at the incipient gnosticism troubling Ephesus. It is not a blanket verdict on natural philosophy, which Scripture elsewhere commends by sending the sluggard to the ant and by having Solomon catalogue trees and beasts (Proverbs 6:6; 1 Kings 4:33). The verse condemns a specific counterfeit: a body of speculative teaching claiming the prestige of knowledge while contradicting the deposit entrusted to Timothy. Used as a slogan against learning as such, it becomes an excuse for the ignorance Christ named as a cause of error in Matthew 22:29.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sheqer (falsehood, deception, used adverbially in the oath texts) and kachash (to deny, deal falsely); Greek pseudomai (to lie) and the prefix pseudo- in pseudonymos.

expand to see more

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, lie, deception; the word in Leviticus 19:12 and in Jeremiah's indictments of the prophets.

Hebrew kachash (H3584) — to lie, deceive, deal falsely; the verb in Leviticus 19:11.

Greek pseudomai (G5574) — to speak falsely, lie; the participle in Matthew 5:11.

Greek pseudonymos (G5581) — falsely named; the hapax in 1 Timothy 6:20, rendered falsely so called.

Greek gnosis (G1108) — knowledge; the noun that the false name is attached to, and the term the gnostics later claimed.

Usage

"“Ye shall not swear by my name falsely” — a false oath profanes the Name it invokes."

"“My people love to have it so” — false prophecy is a market with willing buyers."

"“All manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” — the two qualifiers that define the blessing."
